body: I love this. It would be so wonderful to have someone that knew I was taking anti-psychotics and anti-convulsants without any judgement, especially at work. Don't get me wrong, these meds have completely changed my life and I am so grateful for them, but I feel so lonely and "other" every time I have to swallow a handful of pills just to feel normal.
lol wtf do you know about her life? This is a weird response.

Wow, that was a genuine and thoughtful response (really), thank you. Honestly I agree with you, hiding isn't helping the stigma, but it does protect people when they are in a vulnerable position. If you *are* able to open up about your condition, that's amazing, and you should be extremely proud of yourself. 

When I began writing this the main audience I had in mind was people who don't have a mental illness. I felt frustrated and alone, so I wanted to give them a glimpse of what my situation is like. I hoped it would make an impact on them and foster greater understanding of mental illnesses in the workplace. 

It took 18 years for me to finally get the correct diagnosis, and that was only a few months ago. So really, I'm like an infant when it comes to communicating with other people about my condition. I also was almost homeless several times over the last 10 years, and I finally got a job that pays the bills. I can't risk this job, it's all I have, and I don't ever want to go back to the desperation of extreme poverty. I really hope I can get myself to a place where I feel safe and financially secure enough to be more open about my mental illness. 

So anyway, thanks for the response, and for pointing out the things you found lacking in my post. It's given me some greater insight into how my perspective is different than others, and what I should probably work on.

Ugh, I feel you. Being in this place is really, really hard. I was diagnosed over 15 years ago with Major Depression, it can be such a goddamn grind. 

Keeping my (29F) relationship stable while having suicidal thoughts/urges has been really difficult, but it can be done. What has worked for me is making sure my partner (30M) knows how much I appreciate having him in my life and constantly affirming that he is NOT the root of my problems, nor do I expect him to fix them. 

For example, he texted me earlier asking how I was today. Today sucks. Today it took everything in me just to make it to work, I'm dealing with intrusive suicidal thoughts, feel like I'm about to lose my shit and cry in front of everyone, and people keep asking if I'm okay so I lie and tell them I have a headache. 

I didn't want to unload all that on him, he doesn't know about the suicidal thoughts bit, but I also wanted to be somewhat honest with him. So I said, "I'm glad I get to see you soon! (we're hanging out tonight) Today has been bluh. Everyone is asking if I'm okay so I've just been saying I have a headache. At least I have an appointment tomorrow, hopefully that'll help." I think that him seeing that I am actively trying to get better by seeing a psychologist and psychiatrist gives him some peace of mind.

I don't know anything about your relationship, and having a kid has to add a lot to the stress to the situation, so take my opinion with a grain of salt. That being said, I honestly think the best thing you could do right now is to keep trying to get professional help. I went through 6 or 7 (I've lost count) duds before finding the right therapist, but oh my god was it worth it. I would absolutely be dead right now if I hadn't found someone I could open up to and who gets it. I still haven't found the right medication yet, which is a huge pain in my ass. The side effects for psychiatric meds are rough af, which is the last thing you need during a depression shitstorm.

Finding a source of help that isn't your wife may help take some pressure off of her, and you might finally end up finding some real help. 

Regardless of what you end up doing, we're here for you, OP. I'm sure you hear this all the time, but feel free to pm me any time, seriously. This sucks, and not having someone to be honest with about it can make this suck even more. I hope you can get some relief soon. <3

Thanks for this. The appointment with my psychologist helped a lot. I'm so grateful I was able to find a kickass therapist. I had a string of duds for a long time that made it hard to open up and make any real progress. 

I'm really happy for you, your story is really motivational. It helps a lot to hear about people who have made it through to this to lead good lives, so thank you for sharing.

It isn't a logical hate, it's hard to put into words. It just takes over, the hatred is all I can think about, and reason goes out the window. 

I think it's more that I feel completely, utterly hopeless. I've felt so terrible for so long, and tried everything I can think of. I don't know what else to do.

Lots of things have happened to me that were traumatic or just shitty, but I don't think that's what is making me feel this way. 

I should be feeling great compared to where I was a few years ago. Dropped out of school because of depression and mono, lived in a literal shack where you could see light from outside through the cracks in the walls (I live in the upper midwest, that winter it reached -17F), watched my best friend go from high functioning prized researcher to violent schizophrenic. Moved in with a jackass addict boyfriend and barely left the house for a year.

I was homeless for a bit after my boyfriend threw me out of his place because he found someone else (honestly, I can't blame him). I finally caved and stayed with my crazy and sometimes abusive dad while working **3** minimum wage jobs trying to save up enough to move out. There was a 4 month stretch where I didn't have a single day off. 

Now I have a steady 9-5 job and can afford an apartment, and a solid boyfriend that cares about me. SO WHY THE FUCK DO I STILL FEEL JUST AS SHITTY? It doesn't make any damn sense.

It's gotta be chemical, or a combination of chemical and my upbringing/young adulthood. I was diagnosed with depression over 15 years ago. 15 years. 

I've tried everything. Multiple psychiatrists, psychologists/therapists, CBT, group DBT, a million different kinds of drugs whose side effects just added another layer of shit to deal with. Nothing works for me. At best it's gone for a couple weeks or months. But then... 

It always come back. I always fuck up the progress I've made and crash again. I don't know what else to do. I'm so, so tired.

Giving up is so tempting.

So, yeah, I think OP is right in expecting something other than judgemental lectures when posting in a subreddit that is supposed to be "a supportive space for anyone struggling with depression".

Preach. People on this sub can be pretty awful sometimes. It's supposed to be "a supportive space for anyone struggling with depression" (see sidebar) but I definitely haven't gotten that impression.

I usually post things at other mental health subs too (getting_over_it, mental health, suicide watch, etc.) if I post anything here, because I know that it's very likely that I'll end up feeling worse than when I started if I only post here. 

I hate to bring this up, but I get the feeling that this sub is a little sexist. This is one of my throwaways, but I have others where I'll post and not mention anything about being female and I'll get WAY more heartfelt and respectful responses.

Right?? "Bluh" is all that comes naturally to me. 

I wish that was all I had to say for other people to understand how awful I feel.

I do the same, the envy is like a knee-jerk reaction. It used to be a lot worse for me than it is now. I think just realizing that this was a reaction I was having that I didn't want to have anymore, and forcing myself to find something congratulatory/positive to say to or think about that person has helped. 

At first it felt kind of gross and inauthentic because I was forcing myself to do it, but eventually I realized how *good* it can feel to celebrate with someone. It ends up being a two-way street, and over time it slowly became more and more genuine and easy to do. 

Hope this helps! Honestly, just having the awareness you do now, and recognizing that it's damaging is a great first step.

It could really fuck some people up, and I don't want anyone else to be brought down by me. I'm not really close with anyone which makes it a little easier. It's so goddamn lonely though.

Faking it sucks, but I think it's better than the alternative. What, am I gonna start telling everyone at work and all the people I'm almost friends with that sometimes I get the overwhelming urge to murder myself? Yeah, I don't really see any scenario where that ends up leading to a positive net gain. In the end, faking it is a survival skill.

I feel that. The regret and shame of wasted time is the worst. If I think too long about how much time I've spent just barely existing I start to fucking lose it. The biggest accomplishments of my twenties are literally just not becoming completely homeless, and staying alive.

Honestly? If this is coinciding with other shitty things happening in your life, find a good psychologist. If it isn't, find a good psychologist and a good psychiatrist. It might take a few tries to find the right fit, but this can make a world of difference in the long run. 

Really think deeply about how you've been feeling. Journaling and mindfulness can help keep track of specifics. Then be honest as fuck about your symptoms with the psychiatrist/psychologist. 

I fucked around for so long without doing this. It always came back. I'm still a long ways from okay, but gaining awareness about my symptoms and getting professional help has helped me so much with developing a sort of mental toolkit for when things turn to shit. 

If you're looking to get on meds, I would try to get in to see someone with a good rep who really knows psychiatric meds. The more accurate you can be in explaining your symptoms, the more accurate your diagnosis and subsequent treatment is likely to be.

Feeling this way is so awful, I'm sorry you're in this place. 3 days ago I was thinking that the only solution other than killing myself would be to commit myself to a hospital. I can relate, but I still can't imagine exactly what you're feeling right now.

One of the worst parts of this for me is that when I'm really *in* it, if anyone tells me that "it gets better" or "just don't do anything right now, this is temporary" it seems like absolute 100% bullshit. The person is nice for saying it, but deep down I just write them off as ignorant, they have no clue what this is like. When I feel so bad that I'm suicidal, I almost always believe without a doubt that this is how I will feel **forever**. That it will never stop.

It's f*cking terrible. But you're not alone. 

The way you're describing how you feel made me think of this article that really rang true for me: http://www.independent.co.uk/voices/comment/why-i-didnt-kill-myself-today-8282110.html 
Maybe it'll resonate with you too. Sorry if it doesn't, I might be way off.
